Neonatal spurdog (Squalus acanthias) emerge from their mothers following a lengthy gestation and exhibit a total length at birth of approximately 24 centimeters [Lb = approximately 24 centimeters] at 9 °C [T = 9 °C], a value consistent with earlier assessments by Avsa2001 and YigiIsme2013. Field surveys in the southeastern Black Sea have, however, documented free-swimming individuals as small as 17 centimeters [Lb = 17 centimeters], indicating that a smaller size at birth is possible and that the observed range may reflect maternal condition or local environmental influences. The initial mass of the fertilised ovum within the female reproductive tract is remarkably modest, with the wet weight at start, or the egg itself, recorded at 35 grams [Ww0 = 35 grams]; this figure aligns closely with the oocyte volume data provided by JoneGeen1977. Gestation proceeds slowly in this species, and the age at birth, estimated under a consistent thermal regime of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], is approximately 690 days [ab = approximately 690 days], a duration that underscores the extended developmental period characteristic of many squaliform sharks. The protracted gestation and relatively small size of the newborn pup suggest a life-history strategy that prioritises offspring quality and survival over a high fecundity rate.

As juvenile spurdogs grow, they progress through a lengthy sub-adult phase before reaching sexual maturation. The smallest female observed carrying embryos measured 72 centimeters [Lp = 72 centimeters] in total length, which we consider here as the length at puberty, despite the 50% maturation length reported by Avsa2001 being somewhat larger at 82 centimeters for males and 88 centimeters for females. At this pubertal length, a female will have attained a wet weight of approximately 950 grams [Wwp = approximately 950 grams], a body mass that reflects the significant somatic investment required before the onset of gonadal activity. Sexual maturity in the southeastern Black Sea population is not achieved quickly; under a stable water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], both sexes are estimated to become reproductively mature in their fifth year of life, translating to an age at first reproduction of roughly 2190 days after birth [tR = roughly 2190 days after birth]. This considerable delay before first pupping is a hallmark of a slow life-history pace and contrasts sharply with the rapid maturation schedules seen in smaller, more fecund elasmobranchs.

Mature female spurdogs in the southeastern Black Sea can attain impressive dimensions, with the maximum recorded length for a female reaching 136 centimeters [Li = 136 centimeters]. This ultimate total length is a direct field observation from the region and should not be conflated with asymptotic length estimates derived from pooled sex data. Males of the same population are notably smaller at their maximum observed size, reaching only 121 centimeters [Li = 121 centimeters], a pronounced sexual size dimorphism that is typical of many squaliform sharks and likely driven by differing selective pressures on female fecundity and male competitive ability. The growth trajectories that lead to these terminal sizes are slow, and the longevity of the species is considerable. Field studies, including the work of JoneGeen1977, have sampled females aged up to 70 years, suggesting a maximum lifespan that can exceed eight decades under favourable conditions. In the absence of precise age validation across the full age range, a reasonable estimate for the lifespan, at the prevailing temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], is approximately 80 years [am = approximately 80 years], with some analyses indicating a generational turnover of 25 to 30 years.

Gestation in the spurdog is among the longest known for any vertebrate, a direct consequence of the cold, stable thermal environment the embryos experience. The entire developmental period from fertilisation to parturition takes about 23 months [ab = about 23 months] at a water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], a duration that greatly exceeds the gestation of most mammals. This lengthy incubation within the female allows the yolk-dependent embryo to attain a relatively advanced state at birth, though the resulting pup measures only 24 centimeters [Lb = 24 centimeters] and weighs a small fraction of the adult mass. The energetic cost of such a long gestation is substantial for the gravid female, who must forego feeding for much of the pregnancy while provisioning the developing yolk-sac pups. As a result, females do not reproduce annually; the interval between successive pupping events is often two years, a slow reproductive tempo that makes the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation and slow to recover from population declines. The reliance on a cold thermal environment means that any future warming of the Black Sea could alter these developmental timelines.

The life-history puzzle of Squalus acanthias is best appreciated through the lens of its extreme longevity and late maturity. With a maximum lifespan on the order of 80 years [am = 80 years] at 9 °C [T = 9 °C] and an age at first reproduction not occurring until roughly six years after birth [tR = roughly six years after birth], this species embodies an extreme K-selected strategy among elasmobranchs. By way of comparison, congeneric species from warmer, more productive waters tend to mature faster and die younger, underscoring the role of temperature in shaping these demographic parameters. The largest females, reaching 136 centimeters [Li = 136 centimeters], are likely the most fecund members of the population, though their individual reproductive output is spread over many years rather than concentrated in a single burst. The dry mass of the egg from which each individual begins life is closely tied to the wet weight of 35 grams [Ww0 = 35 grams], and the pup that eventually emerges, at 24 centimeters [Lb = 24 centimeters], represents a substantial maternal investment per offspring. This slow, steady investment strategy stands in stark contrast to the high-fecundity, short-generation approach of teleosts.
